preamble.summary: LXX Haggai is short and stable against MT. Its single direct NT citation is at Hebrews 12:26, which quotes Haggai 2:6 in its LXX form as a scriptural warrant for eschatological cosmic shaking. The Zerubbabel-as-signet-ring promise at 2:23 also feeds into NT Messianic genealogies and the Davidic restoration vocabulary.
preamble.notable_variants: The 'yet one little while' (hapax eti) phrase of 2:6 that Hebrews 12:26 builds on; the 'desired of all nations' at 2:7 whose reading has shaped Christian Messianic exegesis (though the LXX and Vulgate read it differently); the 'signet ring' promise at 2:23.
preamble.theological_legacy: Haggai 2:6 in its LXX-and-Hebrews form became a standard proof-text for the coming 'shaking' of heaven and earth at the Parousia. The Hebrews 12 argument from Sinai shaking to apocalyptic shaking depends on the LXX's specific time-adverb 'yet once more.'

renderings.mt_reading: עוֹד אַחַת מְעַט הִיא וַאֲנִי מַרְעִישׁ אֶת־הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֶת־הָאָרֶץ
renderings.lxx_reading: ἔτι ἅπαξ ἐγὼ σείσω τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
renderings.mt_rendering: In just a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth
renderings.lxx_rendering: Yet once more I will shake the heaven and the earth
notes: Hebrews 12:26 quotes this verse verbatim in its LXX form — eti hapax egō seisō — and builds a whole theology of covenantal stability on its implications: "this phrase 'yet once more' indicates the removal of what is shaken — that is, created things — so that what cannot be shaken may remain."

The LXX's eti hapax ('yet once more') is a tighter, more dramatic formula than the Hebrew's 'in just a little while' (od achat me'at hi). Hebrews's eschatological argument depends on pressing eti hapax as a discrete finality-marker: one last shaking, then the unshakable kingdom.
The whole Hebrews 12 argument — Sinai's partial shaking foreshadowed the final cosmic shaking — cannot be constructed from the Hebrew text alone. It requires the LXX's phrasing.

renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ ἥξει τὰ ἐκλεκτὰ πάντων τῶν ἐθνῶν
renderings.mt_rendering: the treasures desired by all nations will come in
renderings.lxx_rendering: the choice things of all the nations shall come
notes: The Hebrew chemdat kol-ha-goyim is famously ambiguous: 'desire of all nations' (a singular collective — the Messiah himself) or 'desirable things of all nations' (plural — tribute, wealth). The LXX resolves the ambiguity as plural: ta eklekta ('the choice things') — tribute and wealth.

The Vulgate goes the other way: veniet desideratus cunctis gentibus ('the desired of all nations shall come') — a Messianic personal reading that fed 1,500 years of Western Christian Messianic exegesis, including George Frideric Handel's aria 'and the desire of all nations shall come' in Messiah.

The LXX's plural and the Vulgate's singular each resolve the Hebrew in opposite directions. This is one of the clearest cases where the reception-history of a verse diverges depending on which ancient translation a tradition takes as authoritative.
